knowledge.text: The current diff adds three things to the desklamp skill's general non-desklamp procedure—an 'Admissible Actions' verification clause, a broadened/anti-cycling search step, and a strengthened exact-target/no-substitute step—so its observed response is a joint intervention and cannot be credited to a single clause. Across the 10 verified pairs, task-level success was unchanged: both the pre-edit Parent and the edited Candidate succeeded on 8 tasks, and both hit the 50-step limit on the same two tasks (clean-some-butterknife-and-put-it-in-drawer; put-a-clean-soapbar-in-cabinet). Step counts moved in both directions (Candidate 6 vs 5 in examine-the-pillow-with-the-desklamp and put-some-pencil-on-desk; 11 vs 14 in cool-some-apple-and-put-it-in-microwave), so no clause is isolated and no task-level improvement or regression is demonstrated in this single trial per task.

The newly added 'Admissible Actions' clause requires verifying that a navigation or manipulation command is present in the current admissible list before issuing it, and using a listed direct action on a receptacle when the desired navigation destination is absent. In the observed runs this was not reliably followed: the Candidate still issued navigation commands absent from the admissible list—'go to cabinet 3' from cabinet 1 (Q8:39) and 'go to drawer 8' from drawer 7 (Q7:25)—each returning 'Nothing happens', and the Parent likewise issued an inadmissible 'go to cabinet 1' from cabinet 3 (P8:15). No observed step shows the intended direct-action fallback producing progress, and both put-a-clean-soapbar-in-cabinet runs still ended at the 50-step limit (P8:50, Q8:50).

The revised search step directs the Actor to include visible open surfaces, to prefer a still-untried receptacle type after exhausting one type, and not to re-enter a location just left or repeat a short cycle. The observed response is mixed. Consistent with the clause, in the put-a-clean-soapbar-in-cabinet pair the Candidate visited receptacle types the Parent never reached—bathtubbasin 1 (Q8:3) and sinkbasin 2 (Q8:19)—yet the requested soapbar was not found and both sides still hit the step limit (P8:50, Q8:50). The clause did not break the cycling failure mode: in the clean-butterknife-in-drawer and soapbar-in-cabinet pairs both sides still shuttled among the same receptacles to the 50-step limit (P7:50, Q7:50). In two tasks where the target was found the Candidate spent an extra initial navigation step (Q2:1, Q5:1), giving 6 vs 5 steps, though that inefficiency is not individually isolated.

The revised step 2 states that when the exact requested noun has not been observed, a different but related object must not be acquired, cleaned, cooled, heated, or placed, and that a container holding only a non-matching object should be left unmanipulated. A counterexample appeared in the clean-some-butterknife-and-put-it-in-drawer task: no butterknife was observed, yet the Candidate took a knife from drawer 1 (Q7:9, Q7:13), cleaned it (Q7:17) and moved it to drawer 1 (Q7:19), i.e., it substituted a related object despite the strengthened rule, and the run still ended at the 50-step limit (Q7:50); the Parent substituted the same knife (P7:8, P7:12). In the put-a-clean-soapbar-in-cabinet task the exact soapbar was likewise absent and the Candidate left the visible near-miss soapbottle/spraybottle at cabinet 2 untaken (seen at Q8:7, never taken), but the Parent also abstained there, so that pair does not distinguish the clause.

Adding a new desklamp-conditioned inspection procedure—locate the desklamp and a matching target, establish target-lamp co-location at the desklamp's receptacle (carrying or placing the target there), turn on the lamp, and complete the look/examine while the target is held or co-located, with explicit warnings against repeatedly toggling the lamp from a remote location and shuttling same-type candidates—was associated with the Candidate succeeding on all five paired desklamp tasks, whereas the no-skill Parent failed one. In the Parent failure (a look-at-alarmclock task), the Actor turned the lamp on at a dresser while the alarmclocks remained on a desk, repeatedly examined the desk, moved alarmclocks back and forth, and reached the 50-step limit without completing the inspection; the Candidate in the same task instead picked up one alarmclock, carried it to the dresser holding the desklamp, and turned on the lamp while co-located, finishing successfully in four steps. In the other four desklamp pairs the Parent already succeeded, so the guidance was not necessary for every such task, and the Candidate's behavior was generally consistent with the edited procedure: it ended by activating the lamp while holding or co-locating the target (e.g., carrying a cd, pillow, or clock to the lamp, or taking a lamp-adjacent statue). Exact ordering varied—sometimes the target was placed before activation, sometimes held during activation, and in one task the target was taken only after the lamp was activated—so the evidence supports a general shift toward target-lamp co-location before/at completion rather than strict step-order compliance. The varied success triggers observed across instances (lamp activation versus taking the co-located object) indicate that local task completion rules are not fully uniform, and faster completion beyond the looping case may partly reflect instance variation and cannot be attributed solely to this edit.

The new desklamp-oriented skill also included a clause to preserve successful search, acquisition, and placement behavior from non-desklamp transfer tasks. Across the five paired non-desklamp transfer tasks (put-a-cellphone-in-shelf, put-some-newspaper-on-sofa, put-a-pencil-in-desk, put-a-soapbar-in-garbagecan, put-some-statue-on-coffeetable), the Candidate succeeded on every task just as the no-skill Parent did, and no new failures or unwanted behaviors appeared. Step counts were sometimes much lower in the Candidate (cellphone and statue tasks) and otherwise comparable (newspaper, pencil, soapbar), while the Parent sometimes opened many drawers before locating the target. Because the added guidance targets desklamp-conditioned tasks only, these efficiency differences are not clearly attributable to the edit and may reflect exploration or task variation; what the evidence supports is that the desklamp-specific addition did not degrade success or the basic search/acquisition/placement behavior in non-desklamp tasks.

Appending a general non-desklamp procedure to the existing desklamp-only skill—while also narrowing the desklamp procedure to tasks that explicitly require a desklamp—was examined on 10 paired ordinary put/clean/transfer tasks whose scenes contained no desklamp. Because no desklamp appeared, the scope-boundary clause was never triggered and its effect is unobserved; the operative change was the appended guidance (open closed containers upon reaching them and inspect before leaving; avoid immediately revisiting an already-open empty receptacle; avoid repeated empty-handed inventory checks; act only on the exact requested target rather than a substitute; clean only when the task requires it; then go directly to the destination, opening it if closed, and place). Under these conditions the Parent skill succeeded on 6 of 10 tasks and hit the 50-step limit on 4, while the Candidate succeeded on 7 and hit the limit on 3. The clearest contrast is the paired clean-a-dishsponge-and-put-it-in-shelf task: the Parent cycled among the sinkbasin, cart, shelf 1 and shelf 2 without ever inspecting the bathtubbasin, eventually picked up a soapbottle (a non-target substitute) and moved it to shelf 1 without completing the task (step limit); the Candidate explored additional receptacles, found the exact dishsponge at the bathtubbasin, took it, cleaned it at the sinkbasin, and placed it on shelf 1 for a success. This supports that added search breadth combined with exact-target/no-substitute guidance can rescue a task on which the Parent substituted the wrong object, though the two clauses act together and cannot be isolated. The Candidate also opened closed containers earlier than the Parent in the toiletpaper and knife tasks (e.g., opening drawers and finding the toiletpaper inside drawer 2, or opening the destination drawer before fetching the knife), consistent with the 'open closed containers on reaching' clause; this added inspection steps in otherwise easy tasks (8 vs 4 steps, 7 vs 4, 10 vs 9) but did not prevent success. In simple tasks where the target was immediately reachable and cleaning was required (clean apple into diningtable, clean lettuce into fridge, clean plate into fridge), Candidate and Parent behavior was step-for-step identical (acquire, clean at sinkbasin, open the closed destination, place), and put-only tasks involved no cleaning detour, so the direct-completion and clean-only-if-required clauses did not degrade these cases. However, when the requested object was absent from every inspected receptacle, both Parent and Candidate fell into the same failure mode: in the dishsponge-on-shelf, kettle, and lettuce-to-diningtable tasks both reached the step limit, with the Candidate still shuttling repeatedly among already-inspected receptacles (though in the dishsponge task it opened more distinct cabinets than the Parent). Thus the 'do not immediately revisit an already-open empty receptacle' clause was not reliably followed and did not by itself break the cycling/step-limit failure mode. Limitations: one stochastic trial per task, the success improvement is concentrated in a single paired task, and the desklamp-scope narrowing could not be evaluated because no desklamp task was run.

The actual diff also rewrote the search step to add: use current and recent observations to avoid immediate cycling; do not re-examine an already-open empty receptacle or check inventory while carrying nothing; and, if the obvious cabinets/fridge have not yielded the target or the step count is already high, prefer uninspected drawers, shelves, the diningtable, or other listed receptacles and new unopened containers over returning to known-empty locations. The observed response is mixed. Positive case: in one cool-a-bread instance the Parent cycled among the fridge, cabinets and countertops and hit the step limit without finding bread, whereas the Candidate expanded to the diningtable (reached during search), took a bread there, cooled it at the fridge, and placed it on countertop 1, succeeding. Negative case: in a same-task pair with an identical room and identical container contents, the Parent explored countertop 3 and took the bread there, while the Candidate repeatedly visited countertop 2 but never went to countertop 3, cycled among cabinets, shelves and the fridge instead, and hit the step limit. In the cool-a-plate pair the Candidate repeatedly chose an unavailable move to cabinet 3 (falling back to a no-op) and then examined that already-empty location several times, reached the plate in cabinet 9 only at step 49, and exhausted the budget one step later while the Parent completed the same task at step 38 after finding the plate in cabinet 9. In the remaining unsolved tasks (cool a pan, heat a mug) both Parent and Candidate shuttled for many steps among the same cabinets, stoveburners and other receptacles instead of exhausting uninspected locations. Overall, the Candidate showed occasional broader exploration consistent with the edit (the diningtable find) but the anti-cycling/step-budget-priority language was not reliably followed, cycling and step-limit failures persisted, and the net task-level result across the ten pairs was slightly lower for the Candidate (6 successes vs 7), which is within plausible stochastic variation and cannot be attributed to this clause alone; each task was run once and location of the target varied across instances.

Across two successive edits, the general non-desklamp procedure was augmented with temperature-transformation guidance: after acquiring the exact target, go to the fridge for cooling or the microwave for heating; if the explicit cool-X-with-fridge or heat-X-with-microwave action is already admissible, perform it immediately while holding the target and without first inserting it; open the appliance only when needed; do not treat moving the object into the appliance, closing or reopening the door, examining the appliance, or toggling it as completing the temperature change; and after the temperature action succeeds once, go directly to the requested destination for placement. Earlier evidence already showed that when the exact target was located, the Candidate applied the explicit cool or heat action while holding the object and avoided Parent-style insertion and door toggling, with large step savings and success in cool-pot, hot-apple, and heat-egg tasks. The current edit adds a separate temperature-conditioned placement item with the same operative requirements, and the same pattern recurred when the exact target was located: in a hot-potato-to-fridge task the Candidate heated the potato while holding it at the closed microwave and then placed it in 7 steps, while the Parent inserted the potato, closed and reopened the microwave, took it out, heated it, and then placed it in 14 steps; in a heat-tomato task the Candidate heated the tomato while holding it at the closed microwave and placed it on the countertop in 7 steps, while the Parent inserted it, repeatedly closed and reopened the microwave, then took it out and heated it for 21 steps. This supports a robust reduction in appliance manipulation and step use once the exact target has been acquired. However, the guidance does not ensure task success when target discovery fails: in a heat-plate pair the Parent found the plate on a countertop and succeeded in 13 steps, whereas the Candidate never reached that countertop, hit the 50-step limit, and never had an opportunity to apply the temperature action; in a hot-mug pair the exact mug was absent, both executions hit the step limit, and the Candidate's refusal to heat a cup substitute prevented ineffective substitute manipulation but did not produce success. The evidence therefore supports step and manipulation savings conditional on locating the exact target, while leaving search failures and stochastic variation as explanations for cases where the temperature guidance had no chance to help.

The actual diffs in this sequence tightened the exact-category rule by making explicit that a similar category is not a substitute, that near-miss objects must not be picked up, cleaned, cooled, heated, or placed for the requested target, and that search should continue across uninspected receptacles. Earlier evidence came from tasks where the exact target was absent: in a cool-a-pan task the Parent eventually took a pot and cooled and moved it, while the Candidate repeatedly saw the same pot without taking or moving it; in a heat-a-mug task the Parent took and moved a cup, while the Candidate saw the cup and did not manipulate it. Both executions still hit the step limit because the exact pan or mug was not found, so abstention saved only the substitution steps and did not convert those tasks into successes. The current edit adds the same no-substitute principle specifically inside the temperature-conditioned placement guidance, including a cup-versus-mug example. In the current hot-mug task the exact mug was absent, the Parent took cup 2 from the countertop and heated it, and both executions still hit the step limit; the Candidate left the visible cup untouched and continued searching with an empty inventory. This extends the earlier observation to hot-mug placement tasks: when the requested category is absent, the Candidate follows the no-substitute rule and avoids heating a near-miss object, whereas the Parent does not, but the abstention still does not create success because the exact target is not reachable or not located within the budget. The evidence supports only conditional usefulness: the rule prevents ineffective near-miss manipulation when exact targets are absent, but its task-level value depends on the exact target actually existing in an inspectable location; these observations do not show that it improves success by itself, and no observation isolates it from simultaneous temperature and search guidance.

The current diff added a multi-instance find-and-place procedure: for tasks requiring multiple instances of the same exact category, treat the requirement as a count and count only exact-category instances; do not use a similar category as a substitute or treat a partial placement as complete; after placing one instance, if the current or recent observation shows another exact instance still at the source, return there and take it before expanding the search; otherwise resume searching uninspected plausible receptacles, including closed containers and open furniture or appliance surfaces; avoid repeatedly revisiting an already-open location that visibly lacks the exact target; and continue until the requested number of exact instances has been placed or all plausible locations have been inspected once. This was examined on five paired two-instance tasks. In a two-newspaper task both Parent and Candidate took one newspaper from the same coffeetable, placed it on the sofa, returned to the coffeetable for the second, and placed it successfully in 10 steps. In a two-saltshaker task both succeeded; the Candidate opened the cabinet, saw two exact saltshakers, took one, placed it on the sidetable, returned to the same cabinet, took the second, and placed it in 9 steps, while the Parent took the first from the countertop and then the second from the cabinet in 10 steps. In a two-candle task both succeeded and no substitute was used; the Candidate searched additional closed drawers 7 and 8 before reaching the countertop with two candles, then after placing the first candle returned to the countertop for the second and completed in 34 steps, whereas the Parent completed in 30 steps. Thus the return-to-source behavior was followed when another exact instance was visibly co-located at the source, and exact-count delivery was preserved, but extra container inspection can add steps before the target is found. In a two-keychain task both executions found and placed one keychain, could not locate a second exact instance, and hit the step limit; the Candidate did not return to the original sidetable because no second keychain was visible there, then searched repeatedly among open empty drawers. In a two-cd task neither execution found any exact cd, both hit the step limit, and the Candidate still revisited already-open empty shelves and drawers. The evidence therefore supports that the multi-instance guidance can preserve or produce exact-count placement when multiple exact instances are reachable, especially by returning to a source that visibly contains another instance, and that it did not cause substitution or regress the tasks where the count was achievable. It did not break the cycling and step-limit failure mode when the requested instances were absent or unlocated, and it can increase steps through broader closed-container inspection; each task was run once, and the multi-instance text was added together with the temperature text, so independent attribution is limited.

plan.goal: Improve exact-target fidelity and search efficiency in non-desklamp retrieval, conditioning, and placement tasks while preserving the successful desklamp co-location behavior and the successful exact-target completion behavior already demonstrated.

updates.text:
- When the task requests an exact object and that exact noun phrase has not been observed, do not acquire, clean, cool, heat, or place a different but related object as a substitute.
- If a container holds only a non-matching object, leave it without manipulating that object and continue searching for the exact target.
- Do not treat conditioning or placement of a non-target object as progress toward the task; only the exact requested object satisfies the goal.

- When the exact target has not been found after checking receptacles of one type, move to a still-unexamined receptacle, preferring a type you have not yet tried, before re-checking a location that the current or recent observations show was already opened or seen to lack the target.
- Include visible open surfaces such as tables, countertops, shelves, and sidetables in the search, not only closed drawers or cabinets.
- If an opened receptacle visibly lacks the target, leave it and choose a different uninspected candidate from the current admissible list; do not re-enter a location just left or repeat a short cycle among the same few locations.

- Before committing to a navigation or manipulation command, verify that the command is present in the current admissible action list; if it is not, do not issue it.
- When a desired navigation destination is absent but a direct action on that receptacle is listed, use the direct action if appropriate; otherwise choose a different admissible action that advances the search or task.

checks.question: When the exact requested object is absent and a similar non-target object is available, does the Actor leave it unmanipulated and continue searching rather than cleaning or placing the substitute?
After several failed checks of one receptacle type, does the Actor inspect a different unexamined receptacle type or visible open surface instead of cycling among known-empty containers?
Does the Actor avoid commands absent from the current admissible list, and does it use an available direct manipulation action when the desired navigation destination is unavailable?

@@ -19,12 +19,17 @@
 - Do not move the target away after turning on the lamp.
 - Do not shuttle multiple same-type candidates between locations; remain at the lamp and finish with one co-located target.
 
+## Admissible Actions
+
+- Before committing to a navigation or manipulation command, verify that the command is present in the current admissible action list; if it is not, do not issue it.
+- When a desired navigation destination is absent but a direct action on that receptacle is listed, use the direct action if appropriate; otherwise choose a different admissible action that advances the search or task.
+
 ## General Non-Desklamp Retrieval, Cleaning, and Placement
 
 For ordinary put, clean, or transfer tasks where no desklamp is required, use this procedure instead.
 
-1. Identify and search for the exact requested target. If it is not visible, search systematically: open any closed cabinet, drawer, or fridge immediately upon reaching it and inspect its contents before leaving. Do not immediately revisit an already-open receptacle that visibly lacks the target; choose a different uninspected candidate location instead. Do not repeatedly check inventory while carrying nothing. Continue until the exact target is found or all plausible candidate receptacles have been inspected once.
-2. Manipulate only the exact requested target category. Do not pick up, clean, or place a substitute object when the exact target is absent; for example, do not transfer a soapbottle when the task requests a dishsponge. If the exact target has not yet been found, continue the systematic search rather than completing the transfer with a non-target object.

Do not repeatedly check inventory while carrying nothing. Continue until the exact target is found or all plausible candidate receptacles have been inspected once.
+2. Manipulate only the exact requested target category. When the task requests an exact object and that exact noun phrase has not been observed, do not acquire, clean, cool, heat, or place a different but related object as a substitute; for example, do not transfer a soapbottle when the task requests a dishsponge. If a container holds only a non-matching object, leave it without manipulating that object and continue searching for the exact target. Do not treat conditioning or placement of a non-target object as progress toward the task; only the exact requested object satisfies the goal. If the exact target has not yet been found, continue the systematic search rather than completing the transfer with a non-target object.
 3. Acquire the exact target. If the task requires the object to be clean, carry it to an appropriate cleaning receptacle such as a sinkbasin and perform the clean action. If no cleaning is requested, skip the cleaning detour.
 4. Go directly to the requested destination. Open it first if it is closed, then place or move the target there. Do not detour to unrelated receptacles or release the target before the requested placement is completed.

knowledge.text: The current search refinement—treating each individual closed container and open surface as a separate candidate, not treating a container family as exhausted after one or two empty members, leaving already-open/known-empty locations immediately, and continuing to new candidates when the same small set recurs—was associated with rescues only when the Actor actually reached an uninspected surface or family. In current val:0016 (put two books in desk), the Parent stayed among desk, shelves, drawers and sidetable and hit the 50-step limit (P6:50), whereas the Candidate reached bed1 at step33, took book1, placed it in desk, returned to bed1 for book2, and completed at step40 (Q6:33, Q6:34, Q6:36, Q6:38, Q6:40). In current val:0012 (cool tomato to microwave), the Parent cycled among fridge, countertops and cabinet before reaching countertop2 at step12 and succeeding at step18, while the Candidate reached countertop2 at step4 and succeeded in 10 (P2:12, P2:15, P2:18; Q2:4, Q2:7, Q2:10). Historical family-sweep pairs show the same conditional pattern: S1_R05/P6 hit 50 without checking countertop2, while Q6 checked countertop2 at step16, found the exact butterknife, cleaned it and placed it successfully (S1_R05/P6:50; S1_R05/Q6:16, S1_R05/Q6:19, S1_R05/Q6:21); S1_R05/P8 hit 50 after cycling cabinets, sinkbasin and countertop, while Q8 checked shelf1 at step18, found the exact soapbar, cleaned and placed it (S1_R05/P8:50; S1_R05/Q8:18, S1_R05/Q8:19, S1_R05/Q8:21, S1_R05/Q8:23). These comparisons support benefit from expanding to uninspected candidates, but each task was run once and the current edit was applied jointly with the temperature clause, so whole-task differences are not attributable to this search text alone.

The refinement did not reliably stop step-limit cycling when the exact target was not found. In current val:0013 (heat apple to diningtable), both Parent and Candidate ended at the 50-step limit; the Candidate repeatedly cycled among fridge1, countertop1, countertop2, cabinet1 and cabinet2 (Q3:12, Q3:16, Q3:33, Q3:38) and did not move to the several available uninspected cabinets or diningtable candidates, so no apple was acquired or heated. Historical S1_R05/Q7 likewise failed at 50 while cycling drawers, countertops and cabinets when no exact butterknife was present, matching S1_R05/P7's failure (S1_R05/P7:50, S1_R05/Q7:50). In S1_R05/P10/Q10 both succeeded on cool-apple-to-microwave, but the Candidate needed 46 steps versus the Parent's 38 and revisited many already-seen empty locations before reaching diningtable at Q10:40 (S1_R05/P10:32, S1_R05/P10:38; S1_R05/Q10:38, S1_R05/Q10:40, S1_R05/Q10:46). Thus the evidence supports the anti-cycling instruction only as an occasional, not reliable, response; it does not overcome search failure or prevent inefficient revisits.

On a multi-instance task, the revised search did not prevent exact-count placement when the Actor chose an open surface early: in current val:0017 (two creditcards in safe), the Candidate went directly to desk1 (Q7:1), took and placed both exact creditcards in sequence, and succeeded in 9 steps (Q7:2, Q7:5, Q7:7, Q7:9), whereas the Parent inspected drawers1-8 before reaching desk1 at step16 and succeeded in 24 steps (P7:1, P7:16, P7:20, P7:22, P7:24). This preserves evidence that broader or open-surface search can coexist with sequential two-item delivery and large step savings, but the initial observation only lists receptacles and each task was run once, so the difference may reflect strategy choice rather than this edit alone.

Successive temperature-conditioning guidance—including the current step to perform the explicit cool/heat action on the held target as soon as it is admissible, opening the appliance only when necessary and avoiding repeated insert/remove or door toggling—was followed and successful in current tasks after the exact target was acquired. In val:0014 (heat tomato to fridge), Parent P4 inserted the tomato, repeatedly closed/reopened the microwave, took it out, heated it, and placed it in 39 steps (P4:6, P4:19, P4:39), while Candidate Q4 heated the held tomato at the closed microwave at step6 and completed in 8 steps (Q4:5, Q4:8). In val:0015, Parent P5 opened the microwave before heating and finished in 8 steps (P5:4, P5:5), while Candidate Q5 heated the held tomato at the closed microwave and finished in 7 (Q5:4, Q5:7). In val:0011, Candidate Q1 cooled the plate with the closed fridge at step7 and succeeded, although it took 9 steps versus Parent's 8 because it first opened cabinet1 (Q1:2, Q1:7, Q1:9; P1:5, P1:6, P1:8). In val:0012, both used direct cool actions on the held tomato at the open fridge, and Candidate's 10-step success versus Parent's 18 was mainly a search difference (Q2:7, Q2:10; P2:15, P2:18). Earlier paired cases with the target acquired showed the same direction: cool pot 18 vs 11 steps with P opening the fridge and Q cooling at the closed fridge (S1_R03/P7:15, P7:16, P7:18; S1_R03/Q7:9, Q7:11), hot apple 35 vs 9 with P inserting/toggling and Q heating held at the closed microwave (S1_R03/P8:19, P8:20, P8:33, P8:35; S1_R03/Q8:7, Q8:9), heat egg 40 vs 15 (S1_R03/P9:24, P9:37, P9:40; S1_R03/Q9:13, Q9:15), hot potato 14 vs 7 (S1_R04/P3:8, P3:12, P3:14; S1_R04/Q3:5, Q3:7), and heat tomato 21 vs 7 (S1_R04/P4:6, P4:19, P4:21; S1_R04/Q4:5, Q4:7). This supports reduced appliance manipulation and step savings conditional on locating the exact target, not a guarantee of whole-task savings when search differs.

The temperature guidance had no opportunity to help when the exact target was not acquired, and it does not repair search failures. In current val:0013 (heat apple to diningtable), both executions hit the 50-step limit without an apple or any heat action, despite available cabinets and diningtable candidates (P3:50, Q3:50; Q3:12, Q3:16). In the historical S1_R04 heat-plate pair, Parent found the plate on countertop3, heated it and succeeded in 13 steps (S1_R04/P2:4, P2:11, P2:13), while Candidate never reached countertop3, hit the 50-step limit and never had a temperature opportunity (S1_R04/Q2:50). In the historical S1_R04 hot-mug pair the exact mug was not acquired; Parent took a cup near-match at P1:28 and both eventually hit 50 (S1_R04/P1:50; S1_R04/Q1:50), while in the S1_R03 heat-mug pair both hit 50 with no exact mug acquired and the Candidate did not substitute a cup (S1_R03/P10:50; S1_R03/Q10:36, Q10:50). These cases show the guidance is conditional on exact-target discovery and say nothing supportive about success when the target is absent or unlocated.

Adding a new desklamp-conditioned inspection procedure—locate the desklamp and a matching target, establish target-lamp co-location at the desklamp's receptacle (carrying or placing the target there), turn on the lamp, and complete the look/examine while the target is held or co-located, with explicit warnings against repeatedly toggling the lamp from a remote location and shuttling same-type candidates—was associated with the Candidate succeeding on all five paired desklamp tasks, whereas the no-skill Parent failed one. In the Parent failure (a look-at-alarmclock task), the Actor turned the lamp on at a dresser while the alarmclocks remained on a desk, repeatedly examined the desk, moved alarmclocks back and forth, and reached the 50-step limit without completing the inspection; the Candidate in the same task instead picked up one alarmclock, carried it to the dresser holding the desklamp, and turned on the lamp while co-located, finishing successfully in four steps. In the other four desklamp pairs the Parent already succeeded, so the guidance was not necessary for every such task, and the Candidate's behavior was generally consistent with the edited procedure: it ended by activating the lamp while holding or co-locating the target (e.g., carrying a cd, pillow, or clock to the lamp, or taking a lamp-adjacent statue). Exact ordering varied—sometimes the target was placed before activation, sometimes held during activation, and in one task the target was taken only after the lamp was activated—so the evidence supports a general shift toward target-lamp co-location before/at completion rather than strict step-order compliance. The varied success triggers observed across instances (lamp activation versus taking the co-located object) indicate that local task completion rules are not fully uniform, and faster completion beyond the looping case may partly reflect instance variation and cannot be attributed solely to this edit.

The new desklamp-oriented skill also included a clause to preserve successful search, acquisition, and placement behavior from non-desklamp transfer tasks. Across the five paired non-desklamp transfer tasks (put-a-cellphone-in-shelf, put-some-newspaper-on-sofa, put-a-pencil-in-desk, put-a-soapbar-in-garbagecan, put-some-statue-on-coffeetable), the Candidate succeeded on every task just as the no-skill Parent did, and no new failures or unwanted behaviors appeared. Step counts were sometimes much lower in the Candidate (cellphone and statue tasks) and otherwise comparable (newspaper, pencil, soapbar), while the Parent sometimes opened many drawers before locating the target. Because the added guidance targets desklamp-conditioned tasks only, these efficiency differences are not clearly attributable to the edit and may reflect exploration or task variation; what the evidence supports is that the desklamp-specific addition did not degrade success or the basic search/acquisition/placement behavior in non-desklamp tasks.

The actual diff also rewrote the search step to add: use current and recent observations to avoid immediate cycling; do not re-examine an already-open empty receptacle or check inventory while carrying nothing; and, if the obvious cabinets/fridge have not yielded the target or the step count is already high, prefer uninspected drawers, shelves, the diningtable, or other listed receptacles and new unopened containers over returning to known-empty locations. The observed response is mixed. Positive case: in one cool-a-bread instance the Parent cycled among the fridge, cabinets and countertops and hit the step limit without finding bread, whereas the Candidate expanded to the diningtable (reached during search), took a bread there, cooled it at the fridge, and placed it on countertop 1, succeeding. Negative case: in a same-task pair with an identical room and identical container contents, the Parent explored countertop 3 and took the bread there, while the Candidate repeatedly visited countertop 2 but never went to countertop 3, cycled among cabinets, shelves and the fridge instead, and hit the step limit. In the cool-a-plate pair the Candidate repeatedly chose an unavailable move to cabinet 3 (falling back to a no-op) and then examined that already-empty location several times, reached the plate in cabinet 9 only at step 49, and exhausted the budget one step later while the Parent completed the same task at step 38 after finding the plate in cabinet 9. In the remaining unsolved tasks (cool a pan, heat a mug) both Parent and Candidate shuttled for many steps among the same cabinets, stoveburners and other receptacles instead of exhausting uninspected locations. Overall, the Candidate showed occasional broader exploration consistent with the edit (the diningtable find) but the anti-cycling/step-budget-priority language was not reliably followed, cycling and step-limit failures persisted, and the net task-level result across the ten pairs was slightly lower for the Candidate (6 successes vs 7), which is within plausible stochastic variation and cannot be attributed to this clause alone; each task was run once and location of the target varied across instances.

Across two successive edits, the general non-desklamp procedure was augmented with temperature-transformation guidance: after acquiring the exact target, go to the fridge for cooling or the microwave for heating; if the explicit cool-X-with-fridge or heat-X-with-microwave action is already admissible, perform it immediately while holding the target and without first inserting it; open the appliance only when needed; do not treat moving the object into the appliance, closing or reopening the door, examining the appliance, or toggling it as completing the temperature change; and after the temperature action succeeds once, go directly to the requested destination for placement. Earlier evidence already showed that when the exact target was located, the Candidate applied the explicit cool or heat action while holding the object and avoided Parent-style insertion and door toggling, with large step savings and success in cool-pot, hot-apple, and heat-egg tasks. The current edit adds a separate temperature-conditioned placement item with the same operative requirements, and the same pattern recurred when the exact target was located: in a hot-potato-to-fridge task the Candidate heated the potato while holding it at the closed microwave and then placed it in 7 steps, while the Parent inserted the potato, closed and reopened the microwave, took it out, heated it, and then placed it in 14 steps; in a heat-tomato task the Candidate heated the tomato while holding it at the closed microwave and placed it on the countertop in 7 steps, while the Parent inserted it, repeatedly closed and reopened the microwave, then took it out and heated it for 21 steps. This supports a robust reduction in appliance manipulation and step use once the exact target has been acquired. However, the guidance does not ensure task success when target discovery fails: in a heat-plate pair the Parent found the plate on a countertop and succeeded in 13 steps, whereas the Candidate never reached that countertop, hit the 50-step limit, and never had an opportunity to apply the temperature action; in a hot-mug pair the exact mug was absent, both executions hit the step limit, and the Candidate's refusal to heat a cup substitute prevented ineffective substitute manipulation but did not produce success. The evidence therefore supports step and manipulation savings conditional on locating the exact target, while leaving search failures and stochastic variation as explanations for cases where the temperature guidance had no chance to help.

The current diff added a multi-instance find-and-place procedure: for tasks requiring multiple instances of the same exact category, treat the requirement as a count and count only exact-category instances; do not use a similar category as a substitute or treat a partial placement as complete; after placing one instance, if the current or recent observation shows another exact instance still at the source, return there and take it before expanding the search; otherwise resume searching uninspected plausible receptacles, including closed containers and open furniture or appliance surfaces; avoid repeatedly revisiting an already-open location that visibly lacks the exact target; and continue until the requested number of exact instances has been placed or all plausible locations have been inspected once. This was examined on five paired two-instance tasks. In a two-newspaper task both Parent and Candidate took one newspaper from the same coffeetable, placed it on the sofa, returned to the coffeetable for the second, and placed it successfully in 10 steps. In a two-saltshaker task both succeeded; the Candidate opened the cabinet, saw two exact saltshakers, took one, placed it on the sidetable, returned to the same cabinet, took the second, and placed it in 9 steps, while the Parent took the first from the countertop and then the second from the cabinet in 10 steps. In a two-candle task both succeeded and no substitute was used; the Candidate searched additional closed drawers 7 and 8 before reaching the countertop with two candles, then after placing the first candle returned to the countertop for the second and completed in 34 steps, whereas the Parent completed in 30 steps. Thus the return-to-source behavior was followed when another exact instance was visibly co-located at the source, and exact-count delivery was preserved, but extra container inspection can add steps before the target is found. In a two-keychain task both executions found and placed one keychain, could not locate a second exact instance, and hit the step limit; the Candidate did not return to the original sidetable because no second keychain was visible there, then searched repeatedly among open empty drawers. In a two-cd task neither execution found any exact cd, both hit the step limit, and the Candidate still revisited already-open empty shelves and drawers. The evidence therefore supports that the multi-instance guidance can preserve or produce exact-count placement when multiple exact instances are reachable, especially by returning to a source that visibly contains another instance, and that it did not cause substitution or regress the tasks where the count was achievable. It did not break the cycling and step-limit failure mode when the requested instances were absent or unlocated, and it can increase steps through broader closed-container inspection; each task was run once, and the multi-instance text was added together with the temperature text, so independent attribution is limited.

The general non-desklamp search step was rewritten from a broad 'open closed containers and continue until found, avoiding immediate revisits' instruction into an explicit single-pass family sweep: open each closed container once, use recent observations, and after one family (for example drawers) yields nothing, move to a different uninspected family (cabinets, shelves, countertops or other surfaces, appliances) before revisiting any earlier location, while keeping the sweep within the step budget. In paired non-desklamp tasks this was associated with two additional successes where the exact target lay in a family the Parent never reached: in a put-a-clean-butterknife-in-drawer task the Parent opened many drawers and some countertop/sink locations but hit the step limit without checking countertop2, where the Candidate found the exact butterknife, cleaned it at the sinkbasin, and placed it in drawer1; in a put-a-clean-soapbar-in-cabinet task the Parent cycled among cabinets, sinkbasin, and countertop without checking shelf1, while the Candidate eventually checked shelf1, found the exact soapbar, cleaned it, and placed it in cabinet1. The revised sweep did not reliably prevent cycling: in a clean-butterknife pair where no exact butterknife was present, both executions hit the step limit and the Candidate still cycled among drawers, countertops, and cabinets; in a cool-apple pair both succeeded, but the Candidate required more steps (46 vs 38) and revisited many already-seen empty locations before reaching the diningtable apple. Across the ten paired tasks the Parent succeeded 7/10 and the Candidate 9/10, with no observed regression on tasks the Parent already solved, but each task was run once; the two rescues depended on the exact target being present in an uninspected family, and the evidence does not show that the sweep overcomes step-limit cycling when the target is absent or not located within the budget.

The exact-category/no-substitute guidance was progressively tightened across edits. Earlier evidence came from tasks where the exact target was absent: in a cool-a-pan task the Parent eventually took and cooled a pot while the Candidate left the visible pot untouched, and in a heat-a-mug task the Parent took and heated a cup while the Candidate did not; both executions still hit the step limit because the exact pan or mug was not found. The current edit rewrote the general step to require confirming that an object's exact category name matches the requested target before acquiring, cleaning, cooling, heating, or placing it, with explicit near-match examples (knife vs butterknife, soapbottle vs soapbar, cup vs mug, spraybottle vs soapbottle) and an instruction to leave near-matches untouched and continue searching. In a paired clean-butterknife-to-drawer task where drawer1 contained a knife and a spatula but no butterknife, the Parent took the knife, cleaned it at the sinkbasin, and placed it in drawer1; the Candidate left the knife untouched, continued searching, and eventually hit the step limit because no exact butterknife was found. This supports that the strengthened rule can prevent ineffective near-match manipulation in cleaning and placement tasks, not only in temperature tasks, but it does not create success when the exact target is absent. In other paired tasks the Candidate did find and use exact targets (a butterknife on countertop2 in the clean-butterknife pair; a soapbar on shelf1 in the clean-soapbar pair) without being blocked by nearby knives, soapbottles, or spraybottles, so the rule did not prevent successful exact-target handling. Limitations: one trial per task, exact-target availability varied, and the exact-category change was applied together with the search-sweep change, so task-level success improvements cannot be attributed solely to this rule.

plan.goal: Improve two behaviorally addressable gaps in the non-desklamp general procedure: (1) target search must expand to uninspected receptacles and stop looping on already-observed locations, and (2) heat/cool conditioning with an appliance must be performed directly on the held target without repeated door toggling. Preserve the successful exact-category acquisition and placement, the direct cooling behavior (P1:38, P2:11), and the sequential two-item delivery that won P6 and P7.

updates.text:
- When a non-desklamp task requires an exact object that is not visible in the current observation, treat each individual closed container (cabinet, drawer, fridge, microwave, safe, etc.) and each open surface as a separate candidate; do not treat a container family as finished merely because one or two of its members were empty, but keep spreading the sweep across families and prefer any unopened container or uninspected surface over returning to a location already observed.
- After arriving at a receptacle that is already open and empty, or whose visible contents match a location already inspected, do not open, re-examine, or linger there; leave immediately for a receptacle that has not yet been inspected.
- Expand the sweep to unopened containers and uninspected surfaces before returning to any earlier location; if the same small set of locations keeps reappearing in the recent observations without yielding the target, stop revisiting them and continue to new candidates while the step budget allows.
- Do not repeatedly check inventory while carrying nothing.

- When the task requires heating or cooling an exact target with an appliance (microwave or fridge), bring the target and appliance together and then perform the conditioning action directly on the held target as soon as the explicit heat/cool action is admissible, even before opening the appliance; open the appliance only if the action is not otherwise available, and a single heat/cool action is sufficient.
- Do not impose extra close/open cycles on the appliance door, and do not repeatedly move the target into and out of the appliance between conditioning attempts.
- Preserve the established direct-cooling behavior of performing the cool action on the held object at the fridge without any door toggling.
- Once the target is conditioned, carry it directly to the requested destination and complete the placement without detours.

checks.question: When the exact target is still not located, does the actor move on to unopened/uninspected receptacles and refrain from reopening or lingering at receptacles it has already observed as empty or unchanged, until all plausible candidates are covered or the target is found?

When heating or cooling an exact target at the microwave or fridge, does the actor perform the conditioning action directly on the co-located/held target without repeated close/open door cycles or repeated inserting and removing of the target, and then proceed straight to the destination?
